summary: This work develops a subsystem-optimized robust control framework for implementing high-fidelity parallel quantum gates by reducing full-system optimization to crosstalk-robust control over constant-sized subsystems. The method is validated on coupled NV centers, a 12-qubit NMR processor, and superconducting-qubit arrays up to 200 qubits, achieving linear noise scaling for parallel single-qubit gates and order-of-magnitude reductions for parallel multi-qubit operations.
motivation: Crosstalk between qubits severely degrades fidelity in parallel gate operations on large-scale quantum processors, but full Hilbert-space optimization becomes computationally intractable as system size grows exponentially.
method: The system is partitioned into L subsystems, and the problem is reformulated as a robust control task that minimizes directional derivatives $\mathcal{D}_{U_{H_0'}}(H_{S_k S_j})$ representing crosstalk-induced deviations. For single-qubit gates, analytical pulses are constructed via inverse geometric optimization enforcing $\int_0^T r_\mu^k(t) r_\nu^j(t) dt = 0$ for all Pauli components; for multi-qubit gates, the Van Loan integral technique enables efficient computation of crosstalk effects using augmented Liouvillian matrices.
result: On coupled NV centers, robust pulses reduce noise scaling from exponential ($F \propto e^{-\varepsilon M}$) to linear ($F \approx 1 - \varepsilon M$) decay with repetitions. On the 12-qubit NMR processor, robust pulses achieve fidelities $>0.99$ and reduce error accumulation by a factor of 3 for single-qubit gates and 13 for parallel CNOTs. On superconducting arrays up to 200 qubits, parallel CZ gates maintain fidelity $>0.99$ for residual crosstalk $|g_{\mathrm{max}}| \leq 1$ MHz without requiring precise knowledge of crosstalk amplitudes.
